title: Rip currents: escape the pull, help from shore
review_status: Source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
tldr: Do not swim directly against the current. Float to conserve energy; if you can swim, move parallel to shore to leave the current, then return toward the beach. Wave and call for help. A bystander should alert a lifeguard or emergency services and throw flotation rather than enter the water.
steps: Avoid exhausting yourself by fighting toward shore against the pull. Float or tread water if you cannot swim out.
Wave and shout so someone on shore knows you need help.
Get a lifeguard, call emergency services when possible, and throw something that floats. Do not form a human chain.
Check beach warnings and use guarded swimming areas. Calm skies and small waves do not establish safe water.
sections: Editorial family plan: name the guarded swimming area, read the posted warnings, identify the nearest beach access marker and decide who supervises each child. Write the access location in a message before swimming so a bystander can tell responders where you are.

From shore, describe the beach name, nearest numbered access or lifeguard tower, number of people in difficulty and visible landmarks. Keep watching the person so you can indicate their position; send another adult to meet responders if available.
without_help: If no lifeguard is visible, shout for someone to contact emergency services while you look for flotation to throw from a safe position. An untrained swimming rescue can create a second emergency.
household: Agree on direct adult supervision and a meeting place outside the water. A flotation aid is not a substitute for supervision. If conditions are uncertain, choose a shore activity rather than entering the surf.
pack_now: Beach location, phone kept dry, local warning information and supervision arrangements. Do not delay alerting help to retrieve supplies.
next: After a rescue, seek qualified assessment for breathing difficulty or other symptoms. Reassess the whole group before anyone returns to the water.
watch: Do not assume a gap between breaking waves is a safe entry route. Avoid piers and jetties where currents can concentrate.
faqs: Does a sunny day mean it is safe?
No. Read the beach forecast and flags and ask the lifeguard about conditions. If in doubt, stay out.
decisions: Stop fighting the current, float and signal.
Alert help and throw flotation from shore.
scope: Civilian guidance using the linked U.S. reference. Local conditions and services differ. Household planning examples are Osprey Zero editorial suggestions; this is not a live alert or specialist certification.
